title: The blessing
hook: the service ends in a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offering: a basket on a pole, bread up the aisle, and David handing back what was handed to him. Your line was all things come of thee.

Coats are half on. The last hymn is over. A toddler is making a break for the door, and someone is checking a phone. Then the minister raises a hand over the room, or both hands, palms out, and the shuffling stops. Heads bow. Into the quiet come words from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." A few more lines, an amen, and the doors open onto the parking lot and the rest of the week. Before anyone reaches the car, something has been spoken over them. Today's word is benediction.

You met these lines on day four hundred three. Today, where they land: at the door. A benediction is a blessing spoken over people, and a service often closes with one. One often used comes from Numbers. God tells Moses to speak to Aaron and his sons: "On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel." Then: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Kept, shone upon, given peace. These were Israel's words first, and Jews pray them still. Notice who is blessing. The next verse says the priests "shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The raised hands pass the blessing on; in the text, God is the one who blesses. In Leviticus, after the offerings, "Aaron lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them." Near the end of Luke, out near Bethany, Jesus "lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them." Their last sight of him is a blessing in progress. Churches end in different ways. Some use Numbers. Some use Paul: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Some add the sign of the cross. And often, a few last words: go in peace.

Lift one hand a little, palm out, toward one person heading into a hard day: a friend before a test, a parent in a hospital. If you pray, say the old words over them, one line per breath: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee; the LORD make his face shine upon thee; the LORD give thee peace. If you don't, wish them those three things your own way.
Benediction. A blessing spoken over people, often the words from Numbers, spoken as people leave.
Your line: go in peace. The room empties into the week, blessed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christian services often end with a benediction: the minister or priest raises a hand or both hands over the congregation and speaks a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26 or 2 Corinthians 13:14, sometimes with the sign of the cross, followed by a dismissal such as "go in peace."

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples near Bethany, near the end of Luke's Gospel. Jesus is about to be parted from you. what is he doing?
options: lifting up his hands and blessing you.
giving instructions for building a church.
fork.reveal: "he lifted up his hands, and blessed them." in Luke, the last thing the disciples see is a blessing still under way.

chat.says: At the end of church the pastor raised a hand over us. What was that?
options: A benediction: a blessing spoken over everyone as they leave, often the old words from Numbers.
A signal for the ushers to open the doors; the words are just a polite goodbye.
The pastor blessing people by his own power, apart from God; that's what the hand means.
chat.meaning: A benediction is a blessing spoken over people, often from Numbers. In the text, the raised hands pass it on; God is the one who blesses.

notes: First day of a new week (1345–1351).
'Many services close with one' — the outline says often Numbers 6:24–26; the teach says one often used.
'Jews pray them still' — brief neighbor mention (the Birkat Kohanim); confirm wording.
'Go in peace' as a dismissal: one of the Roman Missal's options; Orthodox 'Let us go forth in peace'. Stated generally ('in words like these'); confirm.
Original: יְבָרֶכְךָ (yevarekhekha), first word of Numbers 6:24; confirm pointing and transliteration.
Audit pass: stress in the original's 'say' moved to the final syllable (the -kha suffix carries the accent: yevarekhekhá); confirm against a Hebrew reader.
